Genetic Diversity and Geographic Distribution of
Hantaviruses in Russia
S. B. Garanina1 , A. E. Platonov1 , V. I. Zhuravlev1 , A. N. Murashkina2 , V. V. Yakimenko3 ,
A. G. Korneev4 and G. A. Shipulin1
1 Central Research Institute of Epidemiology, Moscow, Russia
2 Office of Federal Service ‘‘Rospotrebnadzor’’, Lipetsk, Russia
3 Institute of Feral Nidal Infections, Omsk, Russia
4 State Medical Academy, Orenburg, Russia
Impacts
• The study concerns the most prevalent zoonotic disease in Russia and some
other countries with temperate climate.
• The study starts systematic genotyping of hantaviruses in different
geographic and ecological zones rather than sequencing of just few
reference strains.
• Knowledge on prevalent hantavirus species and genotypes at a specific
territory is critical for the development and use of adequate diagnostic
tools, HFRS treatment, prognosis and control.
Keywords:
Hantaviruses; haemorrhagic fever with renal
syndrome; polymerase chain reaction;
genotyping; Russia; detection methodologies

Summary
Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is the most prevalent zoo-
notic disease in Russia. It is caused by several hantavirus species hosted by
small rodents. We describe spatial and temporal patterns of HFRS incidence in
the Russian Federation, and the geographic distribution of prevalent hantavirus
species: Puumala (PUUV) and Dobrava (DOBV). Partial sequencing of nucleo-
capsid and glycoprotein genes of 117 PUUV strains and 78 DOBV strains
revealed several distinct genetic subgroups. The RNA of Volga PUUV subgroup
was detected in patients with HFRS and bank voles Myodes glareolus in the
Volga Federal District, where the highest HFRS incidence rate has been regis-
tered yearly. The RNA of Siberian PUUV subgroup was found in M. glareolus
in the trans-Ural Tyumen and Omsk Provinces, where human HFRS cases have
been rare. During an HFRS outbreak in 2007 in the Central Federal District,
when more than 1000 patients were affected, specific subgroups of DOBV were
discovered in patients and rodents, mainly in the striped field mouse Apodemus
agrarius. DOBV strains might have

DOBV subgroup was discovered in the southern semi-desert Astrakhan Prov-

HFRS cases were diagnosed in this province. Russian PUUV and DOBV strains
have no close homologues among European strains. Our DOBV strains might
be genetically grouped together with Central European DOBV strains isolated
from A. agrarius, but not from Apodemus flavicollis. The Volga PUUV sub-
group is to some extent similar to Baltic PUUV strain, and Finnish PUUV
strains resemble the strains from the Siberian PUUV subgroup. Thus, PCR-
based monitoring and typing provided the opportunity to delineate and expand
the area of hantaviruses in Russia and to identify their new genetic variants.

Introduction
Hantaviruses (family Bunyaviridae) are widespread in
Russia, especially in the zone of deciduous woods and
forest-steppe. They are causative agents of severe human
zoonoses called haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome
(HFRS) (Vapalahti et al., 2003; Khaiboullina et al., 2005).
Recently, HFRS has become the most prevalent zoonotic
disease in Russia, around 5000–20 000 HFRS clinical cases
are diagnosed yearly. The mean case-fatality rate is about
, and 25–50 lethal HFRS cases are registered every
year. Ecological and climatic conditions vary greatly
throughout the country; at least seven species of hanta-
viruses were found in small rodents in Russia, namely:
Puumala, Dobrava, Hantaan, Seoul, Tula, Topografov and
Khabarovsk (Vapalahti et al., 2003; Klein and Calisher,
2007). The first four are pathogenic to humans; the path-
ogenic potential of the rest is negligible or unclear (Schu-
ltze et al., 2002; Zeier et al., 2005). Most HFRS cases
occur in the Volga Federal District (VOFD) (Fig. 1) and
are presumably caused by Puumala virus (PUUV). This is
similar to other Federal Districts except for the Far East
Federal District. However, as virological and genetic typ-
ing of hantaviral clinical strains is not routine, this opin-
ion is based on scanty fundamental research (Dekonenko
and Tkachenko, 2004; Garanina et al., 2007). In southern
Russia and most Siberian regions, human HFRS cases are
rarely diagnosed and animal hantaviral infection is rarely
found. Therefore, the area of the hantavirus spread is
breaking up in eastern Siberia, and HFRS cases in the Far
East Federal District are caused by Hantaan virus and its
genovariant Amur, or by Seoul virus (Yashina et al.,
2000; Jiang et al., 2007). Several HFRS outbreaks in the
Central Federal District were related to Dobrava virus
(DOBV) (Klempa et al., 2008). PUUV is predominantly
associated with the bank vole (Myodes glareolus/Clethrion-
omys glareolus), whereas the main host of DOBV in
Russia is the striped field mouse (Apodemus agrarius)
(Asikainen et al., 2000; Avsic-Zupanc et al., 2000; Klempa
The objective of this study consisted of PCR-based
detection and genetic characterization of hantavirus
strains from widely spread and different Russian regions
with diverse epidemiological patterns of HFRS.
Materials and Methods
Geographic and administrative terms and
epidemiological data
The Russian Federation is divided geographically into
seven Federal Districts Central (CEFD), North-Western
(NWFD), Southern (SOFD), Volga (VOFD), Ural
(URFD), Siberian (SIFD), Far East (FEFD), and adminis-
tratively into 85 units. However, due to historical and

political reasons, the original Russian names for these
units may be different: for example, Bashkortostan Repub-
lic, Astrakhan Oblast and Krasnodar Krai. This difference
has no epidemiological significance, so we use the generic
term ‘Province’ for all these 85 units. A Province is addi-
tionally divided into several subregions (Rayons). There
are usually 10–30 such subregions in each Province. This
minor division will be important when we discuss the
outbreak in Lipetsk Province. Data on the incidence rate
of HFRS in Russian Provinces and Districts are based on
the reports of Regional Centers for Sanitary and Epidemic
Control summarized by the Federal Center of Hygiene
and Epidemiology (http://www.fcgsen.ru).
Patient samples
We have studied blood plasma samples taken from 174
patients with clinically suspected HFRS. One-hundred
and thirty-nine patients contracted the disease in the
VOFD in 2003–2006, and 35 patients in the CEFD in
2007–2008. The samples from 112 patients
were
positive in hantavirus-specific PCR. All these 112 HFRS
cases were also confirmed by an indirect immunofluores-
cence assay. The samples from the remaining 62 patients
were negative in hantavirus-specific indirect immunofluo-
rescence assay, so other diagnoses were assigned based on
clinical and/or laboratory evidence.
Rodent samples
Rodent samples were collected in 2003–2008 in seven
Russian Provinces, which differed geographically and eco-
logically. Rodents were trapped by officially appointed
regional zoologists using either life traps or dead fall
traps. The taxonomic species of the trapped rodents were
determined by inspection using standard keys in accor-
dance with the Reference Manual (Pavlinov et al., 2002).
Animals were dissected in sterile conditions using dispos-
able vessels and tools. All specimens were individually
packed, labelled and stored at
- 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
until testing.
Lung samples of 190 small mammals were collected
in Samara Province in spring and autumn, 2003 from
A. agrarius (39 samples), M. glareolus (32), common vole
Microtus arvalis (75), yellow-necked mouse Apodemus
flavicollis (13), common shrew Sorex araneus (11), Eur-
asian pygmy shrew Sorex minutus (7), harvest mouse
Micromys minutus (3), least weasel Mustela nivalis (2),
European water vole Arvicola terrestris (2), lesser shrew
Crocidura suaveolens (2), wood mouse Apodemus sylvati-
cus (1), house mouse Mus musculus (1), European mole
Talpa europaea (1) and steppe lemming Lagurus lagurus
(1). In 2006, samples were obtained in Orenburg Province
from M. glareolus (14) and wood mouse A. sylvaticus (7).
Eighteen voles M. glareolus were trapped in Tyumen
Province in 2006. Six voles M. glareolus and four mice
A. agrarius were trapped in Omsk Province in 2005. The
samples from these 28 rodents were pre-selected from a
larger collection because they were positive in hantavirus
antigen specific ELISA.
A collection of 390 rodent tissue samples from Astra-
khan Province was gathered in spring and autumn, 2004–
2005. It included samples of A. agrarius (180), tamarisk
jird Meriones tamariscinus (136), social vole Microtus
socialis (33), M. arvalis (23), M. musculus (10), S. araneus
(4), piebald shrew Diplomesodon pulchellum (2), mid-day
jird Meriones meridianus (1) and grey dwarf hamster
Cricetulus migratorius (1).
Lung samples of 146 small mammals were collected in
Lipetsk Province in the beginning of 2007, when the
human HFRS outbreak occurred. There were samples
from A. agrarius (61 samples), M. glareolus (26), M. arva-
lis (4), A. sylvaticus (33), S. araneus (12) and C. suaveo-
lens (10). In the neighbouring Kursk Province, 24 samples
from A. agrarius and two samples from M. glareolus were
collected in 2007–2008.

Results
Since the large HFRS outbreak in 1997, the annual HFRS
incidence rate in Russia has varied within the range of
three to seven cases per 100 000 of population (Table 2).
The regional difference was considerable (Fig. 1); the inci-
dence rate in the VOFD (Table 2, row IV) was usually at
least 10 times higher than in the other Federal Districts,
and the number of cases in the VOFD averaged to nearly
of all HFRS cases in Russia. In 1997–2006, the mean
annual HFRS incidence rate in the FEFD (row VII),
URFD (row V) and CEFD (row I), was about 1.9, 1.5
and 1.2 cases per 100 000 of population, respectively, but
a noticeable HFRS outbreak occurred in 2007 in the
CEFD (row I). Among the Provinces of the SOFD (row
III), human HFRS cases were only registered in the Kra-
snodar Province (row 6), and Volgograd Province, the
latter shares a border with the VOFD. Only isolated
HFRS cases were diagnosed in the SIFD (row VI). The
mean HFRS case-fatality rate is the lowest in the VOFD
(row IV) and the highest in the FEFD (row VII); this can
be explained by the prevalence of PUUV in the former
District and Hantaan virus in the latter one.

The annual HFRS incidence rate in 13 representative

In December 2006–March 2007, an HFRS outbreak
took place in the part of the CEFD. Lipetsk Province was
the centre of the outbreak, HFRS incidence in 2007 being
28 times higher than the historical mean for 1997–2006
(Table 2, row 2). In neighbouring Voronezh, Kursk,
Belgorod, Orel, Bryansk, Tula, Ryazan and Tambov
Provinces, the incidence rate increased 7.7, 4.4, 5.2, 2.6,
25, 0.7, 2.5 and 130 times, respectively. As the result, the
total annual number of HFRS cases in the above-
mentioned Provinces reached 742 cases in comparison
with 190 cases in 2006 and 112 cases in 2005.

Simultaneously with the human HFRS outbreak in
2007, the high hantavirus infection rate was found in
A. agrarius, A. sylvaticus and M. glareolus trapped

Discussion
After China, the Russian Federation is probably the coun-
try most affected by hantavirus infection. At least 5000–
7000 HFRS cases are registered every year, about
of
them occurring in the European part of Russia, in com-
parison with nearly 2000 annual HFRS cases in the rest of
Europe (Vapalahti et al., 2003; Heyman et al., 2008).
Thus, the need for HFRS investigation and control is
obvious. Knowledge on prevalent hantavirus species and
genotypes at specific territories is essential for the devel-
opment of adequate diagnostic tools, as well as HFRS
treatment and prognosis of outbreaks (Klein and Calisher,
2007). The geographic distribution of hantaviruses in
Russia still needs to be further studied and described. We
found only PUUV and DOBV in trans-Ural Siberian
Provinces. PUUV clearly dominates in the VOFD where a
HFRS incidence from 10 to 100 cases per 100 000 of pop-
ulation has been registered yearly. In the CEFD and
NWFD of Russia, the areas of PUUV and DOBV are pre-
sumably overlapped at wide-ranging view but are most
likely connected with certain landscapes and ecosystems
at the local level. This connection requires additional
investigation and careful monitoring. In the SOFD, hanta-
viruses were only found in Astrakhan Province by us
(Zhuravlev et al., 2008) and in Krasnodar Province by
Tkachenko’s team (Klempa et al., 2008). These findings
revealed two new genetic lineages of DOBV, which have
unclear epidemic potential and area of circulation. The
investigation in Russian Far East and eastern Siberia
explored repeatedly new genovariants and probably new

For all investigated regions, the dominant rodent host
for PUUV and DOBV was M. glareolus and A. agrarius,
respectively. The uncommon detection of DOBV RNA in
M. glareolus, M. arvalis, M. musculus and S. araneus con-
firmed the possibility of interspecies infection due to close
living in the same habitat (Klingstrom et al., 2002).
DOBV spill-over from A. agrarius to other species might
be promoted by high-rodent population densities in the
CEFD, where A. agrarius and M. glareolus numbers were
at least five times higher in winter 2006–2007 than in the
same period in 2005–2006. It is not yet clear whether
A. sylvaticus might act as a source of human DOBV infec-
tion. At least, the DOBV infection rate of these wood
mice was rather high
during the outbreak in the
Central Russia in 2007 (Table 3, rows 2, 4). For the first
time, the hantavirus infection of jird Meriones genus in
the wildlife was revealed that expanded the potential area
of hantaviruses to semi-desert zones.
It was stated that PUUV is the most variable of hanta-
viruses (Plyusnin, 2002; Vapalahti et al., 2003). Indeed, a
lot of genetic subgroups were found in both Europe and
Russia (Heiske et al., 1999; Asikainen et al., 2000; Sironen
et al., 2001; Dekonenko and Tkachenko, 2004; Essbauer
et al., 2006; Hofmann et al., 2008; Johansson et al., 2008).
It is noteworthy that in our study all partial sequences of
the M and S segment were recovered by RT-PCR directly
from human and rodent tissues, so they were not affected
by the adaptation to the cell culture. In the highly ende-
mic VOFD, the Volga PUUV subgroup prevailed, which
seemed homogenous at the aa level but might be subdi-
vided into more subgroups (Bashkortostan, Udmurtia,
Orenburg and Samara) based on nucleotide sequence
diversity of
3 \mathrm { - } 7 \%
between Bashkortostan, Udmurtia,
Orenburg and Samara subgroups. This implies that these
geographic subgroups are the result of spatial disconnec-
tion but not physiological adaptation. In agreement with
the similarity of N and G2 protein fragments of PUUV
strains, the clinical and epidemiological characteristics of

these provinces. The question remains whether or not
this rarity is caused by the lesser virulence of Siberian
PUUV subgroup. Finnish PUUV strains resemble the
strains from the Siberian PUUV subgroup but are clearly
pathogenic.
The more DOBV strains are studied, the more DOBV
genetic subgroups are discovered; most likely the DOBV
population is as diverse as the PUUV population. We
found that in Russia at least five geographic DOBV sub-
groups differ from each other at the nucleotide level. The
possible phylogeny of Russian DOBV and PUUV sub-
groups looked ‘star-like’ [all lineages radiated from the
single spot (Sironen et al., 2001)], therefore, no common
ancestor could be identified. Russian DOBV strains had
no close homologues among European strains, but might
be genetically related to Central European DOBV strains
isolated from A. agrarius (Klempa et al., 2005). At the aa
level, there was no significant difference within strains
hosted by A. agrarius, because only small genome frag-
ments were investigated, but these strains were clearly
different from strains isolated from A. flavicollis and
A. ponticus (Avsic-Zupanc et al., 2000; Klempa et al.,
2008). Initially Avsic-Zupanc hypothezied that A. flavicol-
lis could have acted as the ‘donor’ and A. agrarius as the
‘recipient’ for a host-switching hantavirus. Now we see
that A. agrarius-related DOBV subgroups are very diverse
and widely spread in Eurasia, so their origin is less clear.

Our findings confirmed the necessity to discriminate
the clinical HFRS disease caused by classical Dobrava–
Belgrade strains and Dobrava strains hosted by A. agrarius
(Vapalahti et al., 2003; Golovljova et al., 2007). During
the HFRS outbreak in the CEFD in the winter of 2006–
2007, all available clinical strains were genotyped as a
Dobrava-Aa genovariant (Table 3, Fig. 4). The disease

The reliability of diagnostics by PCR depends on
genetic variability for the detection of viral nucleic acids
in unknown samples. The results of this study have
already been implemented in the development of
RT-PCR assays manufactured by the Central Institute of
Epidemiology, Moscow, and used for hantavirus RNA
detection in Russia. Using this RT-PCR assay and
human plasma samples taken at the first 4 days of dis-
ease, we were able to diagnose
of HFRS cases
confirmed serologically (Garanina et al., 2007). The anal-
ysis of genetic diversity and geographic distribution of
hantaviruses in Eurasia may in the future contribute to
better diagnostics and treatment, as well as to a more
complete understanding of the factors that determine
hantavirus pathogenesis and ability to cause human
epidemics.
